text:
Jordan (Sales): Heads-up: large fintech wants a Private deployment POC. Key asks: preserve client source IP + client port to backend (they use mTLS client certs), support SNI passthrough, and avoid app-layer TLS termination at our edge. Can Net/Eng advise best connectivity approach (VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs egress proxy) and what firewall rules / static egress IPs we can provide? @Priya
Priya (NetOps): Quick clarifying q: when you say preserve client port, do they need the original ephemeral port visible to backend, or just the source IP for audit/allowlist?
Jordan (Sales): Both if possible — their backend does port-based auth in addition to cert checks. They run behind an Azure ExpressRoute + TLS-inspecting proxy on-prem.
Priya (NetOps): TL;DR options: 1) VPC peering: preserves original source IP (and ports) end-to-end; requires cross-account peering and routing changes. 2) PrivateLink (interface endpoints): simpler for managed services but typically the service sees the endpoint ENI as source — original client IP/port may not be preserved unless we run a proxy that forwards PROXY headers or use NLB with proxy protocol. 3) Egress proxy/forwarder on customer side (or our dedicated NAT) where we map static EIP + pass PROXY protocol to backend — preserves identity but adds hop/latency.
Ali (Solutions Eng): If we need port preservation, recommend PROXY protocol or a lightweight TCP proxy at the service edge. Example HAProxy config snippet to accept PROXY and forward raw TCP://
```
frontend ft_in
  bind *:443 accept-proxy
  mode tcp
  default_backend bk_tls
backend bk_tls
  mode tcp
  server s1 10.200.5.12:443 send-proxy
```
This lets our front (on the PrivateLink side or peered ENI) pass original client IP/port to the app.
Sam (Platform Eng): Note on deployments: - VPC peering -> needs routeTables updated and no overlapping CIDRs. Works well for low-latency POCs but is more ops-heavy for multi-account setups. - PrivateLink -> easier cross-account security posture; if we run a service proxy that supports PROXY protocol we can keep original identity but we must advertise that to the customer. - Azure ExpressRoute specifics: if their TLS proxy rewrites SNI, we need them to whitelist target FQDNs and not terminate TLS before hitting our ingress.
Jordan (Sales): Good — what ports/addresses should I give to the customer's network team and their firewall admins? Also pricing ask: how much extra for static egress IPs / dedicated NAT for POC?
Priya (NetOps): Minimal firewall checklist: - Allow outbound TCP 443 to our Private endpoints (we'll provide IPs) - Allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53) to their resolver or ours if using split-horizon - Allow NTP (UDP 123) if they require time sync - Ephemeral egress ports for return traffic (1024-65535) if NAT in-path. Example allowlines: 
``
ALLOW TCP 443 => 10.200.0.0/22 (Redwood-private-endpoints)
ALLOW TCP 443 => 34.210.78.19 (Redwood static egress)
ALLOW UDP/TCP 53 => <customer-dns>
```
Ali (Solutions Eng): Pricing: for a short POC we can offer a single dedicated NAT/EIP with a small monthly fee + per-token usage. I'll follow up with a quote.
Sam (Platform Eng): Also add IDS/IPS note: if their TLS-inspectors are in-line and terminate TLS, they must preserve client certs or operate in passthrough mode; otherwise mTLS validation will fail.
deploy-bot: POC checklist created: https://redwood.internal/pocs/1769012345 (auto-created).
Jordan (Sales): Action items: 1) Priya — can you produce a small allowlist (CIDR + single EIP) we can give to the customer by EOD? 2) Ali — send POC EIP pricing and PROXY-protocol guidance. 3) Sam — confirm whether our PrivateLink service supports accept-proxy on the ingress for this customer. I'll sync with the customer's Net team afterwards. :thumbsup:
